What you are looking at

Layers

Volume

Shell

One-station inversion: the pattern is the associated-Legendre magnetic standing wave of each measured mode, centred on the chimneys and scaled by this station's amplitude. Yellow fans are the measured magnetic polarisation (two opposite lobes: 180° ambiguity); their width is 1 − coherence. Not a global map. Modes 4 and up are not in the data.

What to look for

Two opposite yellow fans from Sierra Nevada — the axial polarisation is 180° ambiguous. October fans should look fat (median mode-1 coh ≈ 0.18), not a needle; a rare high-coh column narrows them. Scrub to ~14 UTC: Africa (green) should sit in a fan. ~20 UTC: the Americas (blue). October chimney dots sit south of the equator (SON); June sits north (JJA). Pin tooltip prints az / coh. The globe still says one-station inversion.

What to look for

Grey helix is the month-mean diurnal loop; amplitude comes from diurnal, frequency from the hour-bin mean of fitted mode-1 f. The coloured path is the data (Kp as colour). Compare June vs October: the loop’s amplitude and the hour of the daily bulge should move. A yellow bead marks storm_t when set (Oct 2 03:00 UTC). A path that leaves the helix is a departure, not a fourth mode.

Kp < 4Kp 4–5Kp ≥ 5 nightquake

Spectrum at pin

Correlation, with the null shown

Pearson r at each lag, ±24 h. The grey band is the 95 % null with an effective sample size corrected for autocorrelation in both series (Bartlett). A curve that stays inside the band is a null result, and that is a valid result.
